QF.id: AIFM CIII Governance and Due Diligence_1

question.text: Himalaya Arbitrage Fund, a Cat III AIF, plans to appoint a new external member 'Dr. Arvind Rao' to its Investment Committee whose name was NOT disclosed in the PPM. The fund has 20 investors with total commitments of INR 400 crore. Consent from investors with INR 325 crore of commitments has been received. Under SEBI (AIF) Regulations, can Dr. Rao be validly appointed?

answer.text: No, because less than 75% of investors by NUMBER (15 out of 20 required) have consented.
Yes, because consent representing 81.25% of investors by value of investment has been received, exceeding the 75% threshold.
No, because all 100% of investors must consent for a new external IC member post-onboarding.
Yes, because the manager's own decision is sufficient for external member appointments.

explanation.text: The Logic: SEBI requires that external IC members whose names were NOT disclosed in the PPM at on-boarding can be appointed only with consent of at least 75 percent of investors BY VALUE OF INVESTMENT. Here, INR 325 cr / INR 400 cr = 81.25%, which crosses the 75% value-weighted threshold. Hence valid. The Trap: One distractor confuses the test with 'by number of investors' — the SEBI test is explicitly 'by value of investment'. Another invents a 100% unanimity rule that does not exist. Another ignores the mandatory investor consent requirement for undisclosed external IC members. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C (All-Cat Manager) and XIX-D (Cat I/II Manager) cover the same 75%-by-value consent rule for IC reshuffles. Distributors (XIX-A/B) don't go this deep into governance arithmetic. Manager's Pro-Tip: Keep a live investor-commitment spreadsheet to test thresholds instantly — Cat III hedge funds with rolling subscriptions see value-weights shift weekly, so re-test the 75% benchmark at each IC-change vote; a single INR 50 cr redemption can flip your consent math.
